why_benign: 18 salaried employees remit a fixed voluntary pension contribution to the employer's benefits account on the same day each month. The shape is a textbook fan-in; the amounts are identical month to month and the senders are the same 18 accounts every time.
24 tenants pay rent into one managing agent's client account in the first week of the month. Amounts differ (different properties) but repeat exactly from month to month.

scenario: Charity appeal after a public campaign
why_benign: A registered charity receives 31 small donations in four days following a televised appeal. Genuinely unusual for the account, which is why medium and not low: the burst has no precedent in the customer's own history, and that is exactly the fact an analyst should look at rather than dismiss.

One employer account pays 22 employees on the 28th. Identical shape to a dispersal, opposite meaning: same beneficiaries every month, amounts constant, and the paying account's only other activity is receiving customer invoices.
A wholesaler settles 15 trade suppliers on 30-day terms in one weekly run. The beneficiary list overlaps ~80% week to week.

scenario: Insurance claim settlements after a storm
why_benign: An insurer pays 40 policyholders within nine days of a named storm. Legitimate, and legitimately unusual -- the volume spike is real and an analyst confirming the event is the right outcome.

A cash-intensive restaurant deposits its weekend takings each Monday: four deposits in a fortnight, each $7,400-$9,100. Every deposit sits in the $10,000 band and the aggregate exceeds it, so the detector is right to raise it; the defence is that the amounts track covers served and the pattern is years old. FFIEC's own cash-intensive-business guidance is why this is medium rather than low -- being cash-intensive is a risk factor, not an alibi.

scenario: Car purchase paid in instalments below the threshold
why_benign: A customer pays a dealer in three transfers of $9,500 across eleven days because the dealer's own limit is $10,000 per transfer. The sub-threshold amounts are the *dealer's* rule, not evasion -- but that is a claim requiring evidence, so it stays medium until someone checks it.

A merchant's acquirer settles at $9,900 maximum per batch by contract, so settlements cluster just under a threshold with mechanical regularity -- identical amounts, every business day, for two years.

scenario: Recurring supplier chain with a genuine trade purpose
why_benign: A -> B -> C -> A where A sells raw material to B, B sells components to C, and C sells finished assemblies back to A. The ring is real and so is the trade; each leg carries a different amount reflecting added value, and the retained fraction is well under the 0.5 a laundering ring returns.
Four subsidiaries of one group sweep balances to the parent and back on a monthly cycle. Same legal entity group, same four accounts, documented cash-pooling agreement.

A customer is refunded for a cancelled order and re-places it through a different group company, producing a three-hop round trip in eight days with ~97% of the value retained. Explainable, but the high retention is exactly what a laundering ring looks like, so it should not be cleared without the paperwork.

A conveyancer splits a property completion across five parties (vendor, two lenders, tax, agent) and the surplus returns to the client account. One-to-many-to-one within a week, for a documented reason.

scenario: Tour operator paying and reconciling suppliers
why_benign: Pre-payments go out to four hotels and come back as unused-allocation refunds after the season. Many months apart, and the returning amounts are a small fraction of what went out.

scenario: Crowdfunded equipment purchase by a sports club
why_benign: 41 club members contribute to a named equipment fund over three weeks. Senders are all existing members of the same club with a long history at the bank.

An administrator disburses to 60 claimants over two weeks from a court-ordered fund. Volume and beneficiary variety both trip the shell-company indicator; the court order is the answer and it is a document, not an inference.

Three sub-threshold deposits into one account within a fortnight that turn out to be a tax refund, a pension lump sum and a used-car sale. Sub-threshold by coincidence, not design, and the senders have nothing to do with each other.
A deposit protection scheme releases 9 tenancy deposits to one landlord in a week at the end of an academic year. One institutional sender, nine references.
A private company pays an annual dividend to 12 shareholders on one day, in amounts exactly proportional to a shareholding register the bank holds.
A parent collects VAT from three subsidiaries, pays the revenue authority, and receives a reclaim which it redistributes. One-to-many-to-one with a government counterparty in the middle of it.

A payroll bureau receives each client employer's gross payroll into one client-money account and, two days later, pays it out as net salaries to that employer's staff. Many in, many out, conserved, inside a week -- a textbook gather-scatter -- and the same employers and employees recur every month on the published pay dates.

scenario: Restaurant paying its importer from weekend takings
why_benign: A restaurant banks Monday's cash takings and on Tuesday wires almost the same sum to the overseas importer that supplies its produce, against an invoice. Cash in, matching wire out, cross-border -- the detector is right to raise it. It is medium rather than low for the same reason as BL-007: the explanation is an invoice somebody has to look at, and cash-intensive is a risk factor, not an alibi.

scenario: Franchise cash sweep through regional accounts
why_benign: Twelve franchise stores sweep their daily balances to four regional operating accounts, which sweep to the franchisor's treasury account each Friday. Two tiers of collection into one root is exactly a layered fan-in, but every account belongs to the same corporate group and the sweep is a standing instruction.

scenario: Two marketplaces settling with the same sellers
why_benign: Two online marketplaces each pay out weekly settlements to the same eight independent sellers who list on both. Every sender pays every receiver, so the block is complete -- and it is complete because the sellers chose to list on both platforms, which each platform's seller agreement documents.
